To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
‘To make scientific knowledge become evidence, scientists have to demonstrate the impacts of biodiversity and propose alternative solutions to the decision-makers’.

the adoption by stakeholders of scientific biodiversity knowledge as evidence requires a long-term process of social and political negotiation in which scientists have to demonstrate impacts on biodiversity and propose alternative solutions.
biodiversity knowledge has to be demonstrated to be evidence and that scientists have to be active in social and political negotiations to do so.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way biodiversity knowledge is constructed and the way it can influence decision-making processes.
the question of how scientific knowledge can be produced in a way that it can be considered evidence in decision-making processes.
the question of how to make scientific biodiversity knowledge more effective in policy-making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
scientists should take into account the social context of their research and its implications on the decision-making process.
biodiversity scientists have to be involved in the social and political negotiation of their knowledge and have to be able to adapt their knowledge production to the decision-making process.
biodiversity scientists have to make their knowledge compelling by demonstrating impacts on biodiversity and by proposing alternative solutions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
biodiversity science is not enough to make biodiversity conservation policy, but it is necessary.
biodiversity science is a collective enterprise that needs to engage in the policy arena to become evidence.
biodiversity scientists need to be able to demonstrate the impact of their work, but that they also need to be able and willing to change the way they do their work to be more effective.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scientists have to engage in the social and political negotiation to make their knowledge relevant to the decision-making process.

scientists should be aware of the social and political contexts in which they operate and of the social and institutional processes through which they can make their knowledge compelling and eventually influence decision-making processes.
biodiversity scientists should not be afraid of engaging in the policy arena.
